title: Neuroprotective Effects and Mechanisms of  Cannabinoids in In Vitro Cell Models of Neurodegenerative Diseases: A Scoping Review
content:
Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), and multiple sclerosis (MS) collectively affect millions of people worldwide, and none currently has a disease-modifying pharmacotherapy. Natural, semisynthetic, and synthetic cannabinoids have shown neuroprotective activity in preclinical models, but most remain at an early experimental stage, and their mechanisms of action have not been systematically mapped across disease contexts. 
Objective: This scoping review maps the preclinical evidence  predominantly in vitro, with select studies incorporating in vivo validation on exogenous cannabinoids, including phytocannabinoids, synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists, and cannabinoid-active phytochemicals (e.g., β-amyrin), and their neuroprotective mechanisms across cellular models of AD, PD, HD, and MS.
Methods: This review followed JBI methodological guidance, and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards, with a protocol prospectively registered on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/TAQ9F). PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science were searched, yielding 8,484 records (2,844 after deduplication). Following two-stage screening in Rayyan, 194 reports were sought for full-text retrieval; 176 were assessed for eligibility, and 26 preclinical studies (2015-2025) met the inclusion criteria.
Results: Most included studies were purely in vitro (n = 18); six combined in vitro and in vivo methods, and two used in vitro and in silico or ex vivo components. Studies addressed AD (n = 12), PD (n = 8), general neuroinflammation models (n = 3), HD (n = 2), and MS (n = 1). Cannabidiol (CBD) was the most studied compound (n = 9), followed by the synthetic agonists JWH-133 and ACEA (n = 6 combined), THC and its analogues (n = 5), and WIN 55,212-2 (n = 4). Evidence converged on three mechanistic domains: (1) anti-neuroinflammatory signaling in microglia and astrocytes; (2) antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and mitochondrial pathways; and (3) protein aggregate clearance, autophagy, myelination, and neurotransmitter modulation. Receptor pharmacology spanning canonical CB1R/CB2R signaling, non-canonical receptors (PPARγ, GPR55, A2AR, TRPV1), and receptor heteromerization  emerged as a cross-cutting axis linking these domains rather than a fourth, parallel mechanism.

Conclusion: Cannabinoid-mediated neuroprotection in AD, PD, HD and MS cannot be explained by canonical receptor pharmacology alone; formulation effects and off-target, receptor-independent mechanisms account for a substantial share of the reported activity. Priorities for translation include systematic dose-response characterization, development of CNS-penetrating CB2R agonists, and target-deconvolution studies to establish how prevalent receptor-independent mechanisms/ direct molecular are.
